Overview

OPAL is Oracle's permitting and licensing suite for cities and counties. Every one of its pages had to move from Oracle Alta to Redwood while the code moved from JET to Visual Builder, with more than 50 developers who were new to the product.

This case study covers both halves of my role: the methodology our team used to discover, categorise, prioritise and track the migration, and the end-to-end redesign of one application, deposit accounts, with its owners section in detail.

My role

  • Design strategy
  • End-to-end design
  • Conducting workshops
  • Distributing and managing the team's work
  • Discovery and requirements gathering

Goals

01

Company objective

Give customers a consistent, modern experience that also makes them more efficient.

02

Key result

Improve customer retention and build a base that attracts new customers.

03

Project goal

Move existing pages to the Redwood design system, alongside the JET to Visual Builder code conversion.

Where OPAL sits

OPAL is one of Oracle's industry applications. Inside it, shared modules, setup pages and applications all had to move to Redwood. Deposit accounts is one of those applications.

A repeatable way to migrate 950+ pages

Before designing a single screen we needed to know what existed, how alike the pages were and in what order to move them, with enough structure that more than 50 developers new to the product could follow along.

03 / 10

How we approached it

We brought together business leadership, strategy, product management, design and tech. Postmortems and affinity mapping helped us find the true nature of the problem before we jumped to solutions. Then we ran the same five steps for every part of OPAL.

Deep dive: deposit accounts

Deposit accounts let agencies and contractors hold funds against city work, so deposits, fees, refunds and reversals all run through one account. Within it, we focused on the owners section.

And more

A contractor can become an owner

Owners are responsible for the transactions and projects related to the deposit account. Agency users can:

  • View existing owners' details
  • Add new owners on request
  • Inactivate owners when their access needs to be removed
  • Change the primary owner
  • Remove all owners and add a new one
An account also lets you
Add deposits, refunds and fee reversalsAssociate projects and transactionsAdd attachmentsHold several accounts for several contracts

Usability testing

7customers interviewed one to one
2surveys created for customers
  • Interviews surfaced behavioural patterns and gaps in the application.
  • Mostly qualitative; quantitative research was planned for after launch.
  • Customers explored the new prototypes while thinking aloud.
Understanding the layoutAdding ownersInactivating ownersChanging the primary ownerRemoving owners

Questions we had to answer

Viewing details3 questions
  • Do users fully understand the role of an owner?
  • Will they understand the distinction between owners and authorized users?
  • Do they understand that there can be multiple owners and multiple authorized users?
Inactivating an owner3 questions
  • Do users understand why they need to inactivate owners?
  • Is the difference between active and inactive owners clearly visible?
  • Is it clear when an owner can be inactivated or activated?
Changing the primary owner3 questions
  • Is it clear why users would want to change the primary owner?
  • Will they know who becomes primary if the current one is inactivated?
  • Would they want to choose the new primary owner themselves?
Changing or adding an owner2 questions
  • Is it clear what happens when an owner is added versus changed?
  • Would users struggle if they took an action by mistake?

Constraints we designed within

ConstraintReason

Users can only be selected, not created. Businesses can only be created, not selected.

Users are created elsewhere in the application. Selecting a business is a proposed feature for a future release.

Owners and authorized users can't be merged.

A hierarchy is in place where certain people only have certain rights, so a clear demarcation was needed.

Removing all owners had to be supported.

It's rarely used: only when the current owners are invalidated for fraud, or a team in the company closes.

Four insights, four design changes

Seven customers tested the owners section. Each finding below comes with a live demo of the Redwood redesign, the Alta flow it replaced, and the new flow.

06 / 10
Guiding principle · decision action

Improve clarity in decision making, with enough context and points of recovery.

  • Clarity on decisions
  • Contextual information
  • Recovery points

What testing told us, and what changed

Each figure is a share of the seven customers interviewed. Each walkthrough plays through the final Redwood screens on its own; switch to Alta for the original screens, or to Flow for the new flow. Point at a change to jump to it, or open any screen full size.

Insight 01
71%
5 of 7 people

People understood the roles, but needed some info text to start with.

ScenarioUsers want to view an owner's details and understand the owner's current state.

What changed
  1. A banner on top explains owners and authorized users
  2. Status and role sit upfront on every owner
  3. The primary owner switch is locked, with a proper alternative
Feedback from PMs
  • The new contact card was appreciated.
  • Details are placed in a more organised way.
  • The banner should be closable; it takes up space.
Owners

Swipe sideways to see the whole flow.

1

Walkthrough of the real screens. Redwood: the owners list with an info banner and each owner's role and status, then Amit Singh's details drawer with the primary owner switch locked. Alta: the original owners table, where the primary owner was a Yes in a column, and the owner dialog with a switch anyone could flip.

Insight 02
42%
3 of 7 people

People found it hard to activate previously inactivated users, and wanted clearer demarcation.

ScenarioSome owners' access was inactivated by mistake and needs to be restored.

What changed
  1. Active and inactive owners are clearly marked in the list
  2. An Activate owner action, right where it's needed
  3. Activation asks for a reason and comments
Feedback from PMs
  • Direct activation isn't advised, but asking for a reason helps.
  • The difference between active and inactive owners is clearly visible.
Owners

Swipe sideways to see the whole flow.

1

Walkthrough of the real screens. Redwood: the owners list marks inactive owners; opening Stuart Chime's details offers Activate owner, which asks for a reason and comments. Alta: the owner dialog had no way to activate; people had to add the owner again through Change Ownership and a search dialog.

Insight 03
85%
6 of 7 people

People had no idea who the new primary owner would be until they completed the action.

ScenarioReshuffles in a company mean users sometimes need to change the primary owner.

What changed
  1. The dialog says who becomes primary, and lets you choose
  2. A toast with Undo for recovery
  3. A Change ownership action for the direct task
Feedback from PMs
  • The information banner and the selection were particularly helpful.
  • Unsure about a new button just for this; maybe a future release.
  • An error recovery mechanism could be a life saver.
Owners

Swipe sideways to see the whole flow.

1

Walkthrough of the real screens. Redwood: inactivating Amit Singh warns that Trent Doster becomes the primary owner and lets you choose; a toast offers Undo; Change ownership shows the current primary owner and lets you pick the next. Alta: a plain Yes or No confirmation with no undo.

Insight 04
57%
4 of 7 people

People didn't see that two actions lived in one button, and were wary because it couldn't be undone.

ScenarioSeveral owners need to be removed after being invalidated for fraud, or because a team closed.

What changed
  1. Add owner is its own action
  2. One drawer replaces stacked dialogs
  3. Remove multiple selects any owners except the primary
Feedback from PMs
  • Separating the actions makes each one clearer.
  • Removing everyone and picking a new candidate in one step might be better.
  • The navigation issues from stacked dialogs are resolved.
Owners

Swipe sideways to see the whole flow.

1

Walkthrough of the real screens. Redwood: a plus button opens the Add owner drawer, with owner type and person search in one place; Remove multiple selects several owners but never the primary. Alta: one Change Ownership menu held both actions, and Assign opened a second dialog on top.

Built on Redwood, extended for OPAL

Designing inside a design system meant two jobs: keep Redwood's accessibility intact, and give a large team components that fit OPAL's context.

08 / 10

Accessibility

The designs used the Redwood design library, which was built with accessibility in mind. We were careful not to break its patterns while doing our own due diligence against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG).

Type sizes

Sizes follow the content and stay comfortably legible.

AaOracle Sans Regular, 12 ptAaOracle Sans Bold, 28 pt

Contrast

The lowest ratio anywhere is 6.83:1: AA for all text, AAA for large text.

3:14.5:1 AA7:1 AAA

Keyboard patterns

We validated the designs against Redwood's keyboard patterns.

Tabbetween sections↑↓within a section
Focus stop 1 of 13

The focus order we validated on the owners page. Arrow keys only apply inside lists and button groups.

Contextualising and standardising components

Prototyping got faster once we had context-specific components and agreed standards. Before that, three problems kept slowing the team down.

Recreated components

Components were recreated in different files, so nobody was sure where to copy them from.

Which file should I copy from?

Ambiguous selection

Even after finding the right file, it was unclear how many items to copy.

Which items do I copy to make it work?

Updates in many places

Updating a component in one file didn't reflect anywhere else, so versions piled up.

Should I update it everywhere?

The OPAL toolkit New

  • OPAL componentsContext-specific components, a layer above Redwood's own.
  • StandardsStrings and methods to follow while designing.
  • Kickstart designA sample file so newcomers have somewhere to start.

After design sign-off

Reviews at every level, a close loop with development, and a plan for measuring what happens in the real world.

09 / 10

Reviews, from closest to the work to the widest view

  1. Design teamInitial designs and mock-ups, including gaps and flows.
  2. Design managerDesign principles properly implemented and documented.
  3. Product ownerEvery edge case checked and mapped to the functionality.
  4. Product directorFeasibility, scope of work and customer insights.
  5. Design directorHow the product sits in the design ecosystem.
  6. Product VPHow helpful each feature would be for customers.

Development

  • Validate the plan with the development team
  • Revise wireframes to fit technical restrictions
  • Check QA handoffs and explain the designs where needed
  • Clarify component behaviour in demos
  • Use the design forums as necessary

Monitoring, and what we'd measure

Once the first phase is live, watch real-world engagement on the way to the full vision, and capture customer feedback to start designing for new requirements.

  • Lower error rateHow often people use Undo.
  • How the primary owner gets changedWhich buttons people select.
  • Time to inactivate a userBefore and after the redesign.
  • Time to change or add a primary ownerBefore and after the redesign.
  • Reactivated ownersAnother signal of errors.

Learnings and reflection

What I would carry into the next migration, and what I would change.

10 / 10
  1. 01Cross-functional collaboration was there, but we could have built a deeper understanding of dependencies.
  2. 02Feedback could have come from other design teams too, to learn what worked for them and what didn't.
  3. 03Shorter, more modular development cycles would have brought insights in faster.
  4. 04Error states and edge cases were captured, but a framework with a more rigorous workflow could be introduced.
